name: Karl Kowalski

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and we're not selling anything. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm at Brandt Fabrication, out by the quarry. We make steel brackets, frames and housings for farm machinery. I run the press brake, that's the big machine that bends sheet steel into shape, and I also tend the robot welding cell, loading the jigs and checking the welds. The press brake is a feel thing, you learn how each batch of steel springs back. The welding robot just needs feeding and watching.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Weekends I rent half a garage from a friend's dad and weld gates, trailer frames, log stores, whatever people ask for. I use AI every day, for quoting those jobs, for working out cut lists, and I've even used it to tweak the weld paths on the robot at work, which my supervisor pretends not to know. Marta, my girlfriend, works at the bakery on the high street. Every spare penny goes on tools, so honestly we've got maybe a week or two saved. That's my choice, I'm betting on myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's start with the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say fine, it's a tool, like the welder or the grinder. Use it if it helps you, ignore it if it doesn't. I'd probably post something like 'AI won't weld your gate, but it'll write your invoice.'

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it suits me. The AI helps my side business without anyone big muscling in. I'd keep building up the garage work until I can go out on my own.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working at Brandt for the steady wage and keep doing weekend jobs. I'd save up for a second-hand plasma cutter, about two thousand, maybe by next summer. Then I'd look at going part-time at Brandt in a couple of years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Quite good, actually.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said every spare penny goes on tools. Is that risky with so little saved?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It is, I know. Marta tells me so. But the tools are my savings, in a way. If I lost the job tomorrow, I could weld for a living with what's in that garage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your family think of you going out on your own?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My dad would love it. He had a small car repair place till the big chain opened up the road. He says working for yourself is the only real job security, and I believe him.

S0.say: He'd say AI is just a tool like a welder or grinder, to use or ignore. He'd post a joke that AI won't weld your gate but it'll write your invoice.
S0.think: He thinks a plateau suits him, as AI helps his side business without big firms muscling in. He'd keep building weekend work until he can go out on his own.
S0.do: Keeps working at Brandt for the steady wage while doing weekend jobs. Saves about two thousand for a second-hand plasma cutter by next summer and considers going part-time in a couple of years.
S0.quote: AI won't weld your gate, but it'll write your invoice.
S0.fieldNote: Karl sees thin savings as a deliberate bet on himself, with his tools as his real savings. His father's lost repair shop shapes his belief in self-employment. He already uses AI daily, even quietly on the robot at work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is when people who are willing to learn get ahead. The robot welder at Brandt didn't take anyone's job, it made the ones who learned it more useful. I'd say the same online, learn it or get left behind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think this is my moment. Small firms and farmers will need custom metalwork, and with AI for the design and quotes, I can do it faster than the big shops. Brandt might cut people, but I'd want to be gone by then anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd push hard on the garage business, get a proper website the AI builds, and buy the plasma cutter on finance if I have to. I'd ask Brandt to train me fully on the robot programming, so I learn it on their money. Within the year I'd want weekend work bringing in half my wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Excited. A bit nervous about the money, but mostly fired up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the robot welder didn't take anyone's job. Is that true?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Well, it took Gary's job on the manual line, and he went to the warehouse. So not exactly true. But the people who learned it got a bit more money. I suppose I tell it the way that suits me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Finance on a plasma cutter with a week or two saved. What if it went wrong?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd sell the cutter and lose a bit. Marta would kill me. But I'd rather try and lose a few hundred than sit at Brandt waiting to be told I'm surplus.

S1.say: He'd say this is when people willing to learn get ahead, citing the robot welder at Brandt as making learners more useful. He'd post the same online: learn it or get left behind.
S1.think: He sees steady disruption as his moment, with AI letting him do custom metalwork faster than big shops. If Brandt cuts people, he'd want to be gone already.
S1.do: Grows the garage business with an AI-built website and buys a plasma cutter on finance if needed. Gets fully trained on robot programming at Brandt's expense and aims for weekend work to bring in half his wage within a year.
S1.feel: Excited and fired up, a bit nervous about money.
S1.quote: So not exactly true. But the people who learned it got a bit more money. I suppose I tell it the way that suits me.
S1.fieldNote: Karl caught himself overstating the robot welder story and admitted it cost a colleague his job. He is happy to take financial risk with almost no savings. His free-market outlook shows in 'learn it or get left behind', delivered with real energy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's the market, and you can't stop it, but nobody can adapt in two years. I'd say government should keep out of the way of small businesses and let us try things. I'd still say learn the tools.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it scares me more than I'd admit. If AI and robots can do almost any work cheaper, then a big firm with a robot fab cell beats my garage on every gate. My whole plan was to be faster than the big shops, and I wouldn't be.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go all in on my own business straight away while people still want a person, and try to buy a second-hand robot welder myself, if I could get the money. Marta and I would cut everything else. If that didn't work, I'd look at doing installations and repairs on robots, because someone has to get them running at first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared and hyped at the same time. Mostly scared, if I'm honest, because I've got no cushion.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With only 2 years' warning, could you raise the money for a robot welder?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably not. Maybe a loan, but banks don't lend to a guy with a garage and a week's savings. That's the thing, the people with money buy the robots and win.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said government should keep out of the way. Would you take help if it came?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If it was help to start a business, a loan or a grant for tools, yes. If it was money for sitting at home, I'd hate it. I'd probably take it anyway if Marta needed it.

S2.say: He'd say it's the market and can't be stopped, but no one can adapt in two years. He'd want government to stay out of small businesses' way and would still urge people to learn the tools.
S2.think: He's more scared than he'd admit, because a big firm with robot fabrication would beat his garage on every job. His plan of being faster than big shops would no longer work.
S2.do: Goes all in on his own business and tries to buy a second-hand robot welder, cutting all other spending with Marta. Falls back on installing and repairing robots if that fails.
S2.feel: Scared and hyped at once, mostly scared with no cushion.
S2.quote: My whole plan was to be faster than the big shops, and I wouldn't be.
S2.fieldNote: Karl's confidence breaks when he sees that capital, not skill, decides who wins. He'd welcome a business loan or grant but dislikes benefits, though he'd take them for Marta. The fast scenario exposes how thin his cushion really is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough for people who hustle. Learn the robots, start something, don't wait for a handout. I'd still say it the same way, at work and online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years gives me a real window. I could build the business for three years, buy my own robot cell, and be the small guy who owns the machines instead of the guy replaced by them. It's tight, but it's possible.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year, plasma cutter, website, and go part-time at Brandt. By year two, a small unit on the industrial estate and a used robot welder, financed against my orders. I'd save every bit of profit, not spend it on a nicer van.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nervous, but it's the good kind, like before a big job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the big firms still undercut you by year five?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd sell the kit and I'd have something to sell, which is more than a wage gives you. I'd rather own a robot that's worth something than nothing at all.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Marta say about all that risk?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She'd want us to get married first, honestly, and do things properly. Her family's very traditional, same as mine. I'd probably propose in year one, and the wedding would be small so the money goes into the unit.

S3.say: He'd say five years is enough for people who hustle: learn the robots, start something and don't wait for handouts. He'd say it at work and online.
S3.think: He sees five years as a real window to build his business and buy his own robot cell, becoming the owner rather than the replaced. It's tight but possible.
S3.do: Buys a plasma cutter, builds a website and goes part-time at Brandt in the first year. Rents a small unit and finances a used robot welder by year two, saving all profit instead of upgrading his van.
S3.feel: Nervous in a good way, like before a big job.
S3.quote: Be the small guy who owns the machines instead of the guy replaced by them.
S3.fieldNote: Karl's plan with five years is about ownership: owning the robots rather than being replaced by them. He'd propose to Marta and keep the wedding small to fund the unit. His traditional values show in wanting to marry before taking big risks together.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty. Anyone who wants to work can retrain or start something. Apprenticeships, small businesses, families backing each other, that's how it should go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, ten years is the dream version for me. I could build a proper fab shop with a few robots and a couple of lads I've trained. When AGI arrives, I'd own something, and that matters more than any job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Like the five-year one, but slower and safer. Grow the garage first, save six months properly, then the unit and the robot around year three. I'd take on an apprentice by year four, because I'd want to do for someone what nobody did for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly confident. There's a question mark at the end, but I'd be standing on my own feet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd own something when AGI arrives. Would that still be worth much?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't know. If robots make everything cheap, maybe my robots aren't worth much either. But owning something is still better than being owed nothing. That's what my dad would say.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why take on an apprentice if AI could do the work by then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because some kid's going to need someone to show him how to weld and run a business, robots or not. Maybe he ends up running robots. Maybe he ends up doing something we haven't thought of. Either way, somebody should give him a start.

S4.say: He'd say ten years is plenty for anyone willing to work to retrain or start something, through apprenticeships, small businesses and family support.
S4.think: He sees ten years as the dream version: building a proper fab shop with robots and staff he's trained. Owning something when AGI arrives matters more to him than any job.
S4.do: Grows the garage business, builds six months of savings, then rents a unit and buys a robot around year three. Takes on an apprentice by year four.
S4.feel: Mostly confident, with a question mark at the end.
S4.quote: Owning something is still better than being owed nothing. That's what my dad would say.
S4.fieldNote: Karl sees AGI mainly as a chance to own capital rather than as a threat to a wage. He admitted that robots might lose value too but holds to ownership as a principle. Wanting to give an apprentice a start shows a generous side beneath the hustle talk.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because the people with money buy the robots and win, and I wouldn't have the money in time. What would help is loans or grants for small businesses to buy machines, and apprenticeships so young people learn trades from real people. I want a leg up, not a cheque.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask who'll own the robots. I want it to be people like me, small shops in small towns, not just three giant companies. That's the bit that decides whether this is good or bad.

headlineQuote: The tools are my savings, in a way. If I lost the job tomorrow, I could weld for a living with what's in that garage.
portrait: Karl is a 27-year-old press brake operator and robot welding cell tender at a steel fabrication shop by the quarry, living with his girlfriend Marta, a bakery worker, with a week or two saved because every spare penny goes on tools for his weekend welding business. He uses AI daily and believes in self-reliance and free markets, shaped by his father's lost repair shop. He sees steady change as his moment and is honest when he bends the story to suit himself. Fast AGI frightens him because capital, not skill, would decide who wins, while ten years lets him dream of owning his own robot fab shop and training an apprentice.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because people with money would buy the robots and win, and he wouldn't have the money in time.
whatWouldHelp: Loans or grants for small businesses to buy machines, and apprenticeships so young people learn trades from real people.
